56 
Loop:
57	
58	- Make api call
59	- Get response
60	- Add the response to conversation history
61	
62	If response contains function call:
63	
64	- Execute function call
65	- Add the function call output to history
66	- Continue
67	
68	If not:
69	
70	- Break
71
72 73 There are factors that can break the loop other than response completion: guardrails, errors, context limit, billing etc. 74 75 ## Components of Agent Harness: 76 77 1. Harness Initializer 78 2. Interaction Loop 79 3. Autonomous Loop 80 4. Tools 81 5. State Management 82 6. Parsing 83 7. Context Management 84 8. Guardrails 85 9. Error Handling 86 87 Other components (we will not talk about these): 88 89 10. Memory 90 11. Subagent 91 12. Verification Layer 92 13. MCP 93 14. Skills 94 95 ### 1. Harness Initializer 96 97 It parses the cli command and initializes conversation history, model, allowed tools, output formats, permission modes, effort/thinking level, interface etc. 98 99 100 101 ### 2. Interaction Loop 102 103 Harness contains two major loops: 104 105 - Outer: Interaction loop 106 - Inner: Autonomous Loop 107 108 Interaction loop asks for input, checks token usage, and handles user message queue. 109 110 It verifies if queue has items before asking for new input. 111 112 User message is constructed in structured format and added to the conversation history. 113 114 ```python 115 { 116 "role": "user", 117 "content": [ 118 { 119 "type": "input_text", 120 "text": "Say hello world", 121 } 122 ], 123 } 124 ``` 125 126 If with in the context limit, it runs agent loop. 127 128 In case it hits the limit, the user message is added in the queue. Then a compaction message is constructed, added to the conversation history, and runs agent loop. 129 130 ```python 131 { 132 "role": "user", 133 "content": [ 134 { 135 "type": "input_text", 136 "text": "Create a concise continuation summary of the conversation", 137 } 138 ], 139 } 140 ``` 141 142 Apart from function call, compaction run also sets the condition to continue the agent loop. 143 144 ### 3. Autonomous Loop 145 146 This inner loop communicates with the LLM provider, and runs autonomously until it needs feedback from the user. It: 147 148 1. Checks context limit and handles compaction. 149 2. Makes api call to the LLM provider 150 3. Streams responses 151 4. Parses responses 152 5. Asks approval for function call 153 6. Executes functions 154 7. Adds responses and function call output to conversation history 155 8. Determines whether to continue or break the loop. 156 157 ### 4. Tools 158 159 Tools allow models perform action. For an agent harness, core tools can be: 160 161 - Read 162 - Write 163 - Edit 164 - Bash 165 166 To make it even better: 167 168 - File search (A fast file finder using fff or ripgrep) 169 - To-do (Good for keeping models in check for long running, and multi-step task) 170 - Web search (Included in the models) 171 172 ### 5. State Management 173 174 OpenAI responses api, Anthropic messages api are all stateless. 175 176 It means every api request made is a new request with no stored data of existing api calls. You need to include the full conversation history in every request. 177 178 Store the events like user messages, assistant responses, function call request, function call output in memory and in a jsonl file for persistent data. 179 180 Stored events in jsonl will allow you to later resume a conversation, fork a session, and branch it out from a specific message. 181 182 ### 6. Parsing 183 184 You need to parse the server sent events (SSE) or the response. Parsing allows you to simplify complex structures. It also ensures you only get what you have defined. 185 186 Harnesses can be provider agnostic. Construct it in a general structure if you support multiple ai providers. 187 188 ### 7. Context Management 189 190 Model performance degrades as the context window fills up. You can set the usable context limit to 50–80% of the context window model supports. Once it goes beyond that trigger compaction. 191 192 Compaction is creating a brief summary of the conversation. 193 194 You can use a simple summary prompt, make api request. Then clear the conversation history and insert the summary. 195 196 OpenAI allows server side compaction. You set the usable context limit. Once the limit hits, it summarizes the conversation and returns the summary. Parse the summary event, clear history and insert it. 197 198 ### 8. Guardrails 199 200 Agent harnesses with tools can access unauthorized files, can run destructive commands. A set of guardrails helps keep things safe. Few things you can do to ensure safety: 201 202 - Limiting access to current working directory 203 - Ask approvals before executing tools that's not on allowed list 204 - Trigger error on a set of keywords in user message 205 - Limit web search to specified websites 206 - Run the agent in a Sandbox 207 208 Models can run forever, limiting it to a certain steps can help save token wastage. 209 210 ### 9. Error Handling 211 212 Function calls can fail. The arguments passed might not be a valid value, or structured properly. 213 214 You can build the function call output and pass the error in the result to inform the model. 215 216 ```python 217 { 218 "type": "function_call_output", 219 "call_id": "rand_123", 220 "output": '{ "error": "error msg" }', 221 } 222 ``` 223 224 This helps model learn and retry with a different value. 225 226 Implement retry with exponential backoff for network failures or api failures. 227 228 > Skip next section if you understand function calling 229 230 ## Function Calling 231 232 Function calling (aka tool call) extends model capability. It gives model access to external functions and data. 233 234 **1. Define a function.** 235 e.g read_file that takes 'path' as an argument and returns the contents of the file. 236 237 ```py 238 def read_file(path: str) -> str: ... 239 ``` 240 241 **2. Inform AI using function definition.** 242 Function definition contains function name, description, and the arguments you want AI to send to execute the function. 243 244 Simplified example: 245 246 ```python 247 def_read_file = { 248 "name": "read_file", 249 "description": "reads the content of the file", 250 "parameters": { 251 "properties": { 252 "path": { 253 "type": "string", 254 "description": "path to read", 255 }, 256 } 257 }, 258 } 259 ``` 260 261 Function definition is then passed in the body when making api request. 262 263 ```python 264 { 265 "model": "gpt-5.6-sol", 266 "input": "prompt here", 267 "tools": [def_read_file], 268 "stream": True, 269 } 270 ``` 271 272 **3. Models don't execute function on its own.** 273 It sends a response of type 'function call' and contains: 274 275 - Name 276 - Id 277 - Arguments 278 279 ```python 280 { 281 "type": "function_call", 282 "call_id": "rand_123", 283 "name": "read_file", 284 "path": "/src/hello_world.rs", 285 } 286 ``` 287 288 **4. Parse and execute.** 289 We parse the function call and execute the matching function with the ai provided argument. 290 291 ```python 292 path = event.get("path") 293 contents = read_file("/src/hello_world.rs") 294 ``` 295 296 5. Add output to conversation history and make new api request. Output include: 297 298 - Event type 299 - Call id (from function_call event) 300 - Output (plain string or json) 301 302 ```python 303 { 304 "type": "function_call_output", 305 "call_id": "rand_123", 306 "output": '{ "contents": "contents here" }', 307 } 308 ``` 309 310 ## Harness Interfaces 311 312 Agent harness contains multiple ways to interact with it. 313 314 Interactive: 315 316 - Terminal User Interface (TUI) 317 318 ![Opencode](/open-code-tmp.png) 319 320 Programmatic: 321 322 - One shot exec: Executes a single prompt and exits. e.g claude -p 'say hello' 323 - Json stream: Runs a persistent session and streams json events. 324 - Standalone server. Spins up a server that you can interact over JSON-RPC. e.g codex exec-server 325 326 ## Build Your Own Agent Harness 327 328 Start small. Don't try to build claude code. Build a small set of components, tools, and simplified functionalities. You can see the [agent harness I built](https://github.com/yogesharc/mimi) for reference. 329

1	---
2	title: "What 6 Months of Building a SaaS Taught Me"
3	meta_title: "What 6 Months of Building a SaaS Taught Me"
4	meta_description: "Actionable lessons, insights, and hard truths on building a product, operation, and life."
5	published_date: "2026-01-02"
6	modified_date: "2026-01-02"
7	---
8	
9	Actionable lessons, insights, and hard truths on building a product, operation, and life.
10	
11	I spent the last 6 months building [Promptmonitor](https://www.promptmonitor.io). Here's what I learned:
12	
13	1. **Early growth comes in bursts:** we barely had revenue for first few months. We were stuck at the same MRR for months, nothing was working. Then we doubled in a month. Then grew another 50% the next. Growth doesn't come gradually, it comes in bursts.
14	
15	2. **[Product > Distribution:](https://x.com/yogesharc/status/1988271189060681996)** a lot of people talk about distribution, and good distribution helps. Distribution becomes easier when the product is good. If it's not, no amount of marketing is going to help you.
16	
17	3. **Stop building and start marketing:** once you have built the core features, focus on fixing bugs and marketing. Try out a few channels, see what works. Once you find the channel that works for you, double down on it. Read 'Traction' by Gabriel Weinberg and Justin Mares. This book helped me, it's full of actionable ideas.
18	
19	4. **Track your funnel, iterate weekly:** implement web analytics immediately. Set up a funnel: how many people land on site → sign up → start a trial → convert. Every week, look at the numbers. Find your biggest drop-off point. Create a hypothesis for why people are dropping off, then test a fix next week. I changed things on Sunday and Monday, since I'm in Nepal I could build before the week started in US and EU. Sometimes it's confusing copy on pricing. Sometimes it's the placement of things. Sometimes it's the entire onboarding flow. Keep experimenting until something works, then keep that.
20	
21	   I used to do this manually every week, pulling numbers from web analytics, Stripe, signups, trials, Google Search Console, all into a Google sheet. It was tedious but necessary. I'm now building [Supalytics](https://www.supalytics.co) to make this easier, web analytics with revenue attribution so you can see which channels are actually bringing in money.
22	
23	5. **Users are (often) dumb:** keep your app simple and easy to use. Work on the flows and ux. Reduce friction as much as possible, don't ask them to fill in too much info. Even the simplest thing that makes sense to you, users don't get it. Check Session replays, if you see them dropping off, not understanding the app, flows, not reaching different features or pages rework on it.
24	
25	6. **Emerging markets are high risk, high reward:** in a new market, a lot of them are trying out multiple tools at the same time. They're not just looking for a solution, they're starting trials for every competitor simultaneously. Retention is harder when everyone is comparison shopping. But the opportunity is equally big. Every company, even the big ones, are trying to figure out and adopt these new tools. If your product is good and you can close, you have a real shot at landing clients you'd never reach in a mature market. The risk and the opportunity are on the same level.
26	
27	7. **Experiment with pricing:** at early stage, you need to constantly experiment with pricing, some customers happily pay $200/mo, some say $29 is expensive. Either you are reaching the wrong audience, or the ROI doesn't justify the price, or the profit margins are too high. Unless you understand the market, and your ICP, it's going to take some time to figure out pricing. We are still trying to figure this out.
28	
29	8. **Things break all the time:** no app is free of bugs, but bugs are not an issue. It's only the problem when it exists and you don't know about it. Sometimes there can be bug in onboarding, or payment, and you don't get new trials, customers etc. These things need to be tested time and again. Just keep an eye on Stripe, signups, onboarding_status, error rate in Vercel, and whether webhooks are getting resolved.
30	
31	9. **Make it easy for people to communicate with you:** add live chat. Some people will inform you about bugs, and they really want to use the app. If someone goes out of their way to report a bug, that's a signal you're building something they actually want.
